PL-2 requires system security and privacy plans to describe the operational context of the system in terms of mission and business processes and to define constituent system components. This supports understanding of organizational outcomes and capabilities at the system level.

PM-28 Risk Framing identifies and documents assumptions, constraints, priorities, and trade-offs that shape how risk responses cover organizational requirements and risks, directly supporting strategy coverage review.

PL-2 requires developing security and privacy plans that are consistent with the enterprise architecture, explicitly define components, and describe operational context. The plan development and dissemination process supports the communication element of the policy.

PM-31 Continuous Monitoring Strategy establishes organization-wide metrics, monitoring frequencies, and assessment frequencies that detect changes in threats, requirements, and technology, enabling the policy to be refreshed accordingly.

PM-9 Risk Management Strategy develops a comprehensive strategy to manage security risk to organizational operations and assets, addressing the policy foundation for cybersecurity risk management. However, it does not explicitly cover the review/update/communicate/enforce lifecycle on its own.

PM-1 requires developing and disseminating an organization-wide information security program plan describing security program management controls. The program plan typically encompasses risk management objectives that are agreed upon across the organization.

PM-28 (Risk Framing) requires identifying and documenting assumptions, constraints, priorities, and trade-offs for managing risk. This establishes the foundation needed to formulate risk management objectives but does not by itself document stakeholder agreement.

PM-28 (Risk Framing) requires identifying and documenting priorities and trade-offs considered by the organization for managing risk. These directly inform risk appetite and tolerance but the control does not mandate formal, communicated, maintained statements.

PM-1 develops and disseminates an organization-wide information security program plan that addresses roles, responsibilities, and management commitment — supporting establishment and communication of cybersecurity roles.

PM-29 aligns information security and privacy management processes with 'strategic, operational, and budgetary planning processes,' supporting resource allocation aligned with risk strategy.

AT-2 provides security and privacy literacy training to system users as part of initial training and at defined frequency thereafter, supporting inclusion of cybersecurity in ongoing personnel/HR practices.

PM-4 requires a process for plans of action and milestones that explicitly covers the supply chain risk management program alongside security and privacy, supporting integration across programs.

PM-6 requires developing, monitoring, and reporting on measures of performance for information security and privacy, supplying the measurement mechanism that supports performance monitoring of supply chain practices.
SA-10 requires developer configuration management during design, development, implementation, operation, and disposal, supporting lifecycle-wide coverage of supply chain components.

SA-22 explicitly requires replacing system components when support is no longer available from the developer/vendor/manufacturer, directly addressing the 'replaced commensurate with risk' aspect for software components.

MA-2 requires scheduling, documenting, and reviewing maintenance, repair, and replacement records; approving and monitoring maintenance activities — directly addressing hardware maintenance and replacement.
MA-6 requires obtaining maintenance support and/or spare parts for system components within a defined time period of failure, ensuring timely hardware maintenance.

SA-22 requires replacing system components (including hardware) when support is no longer available from the developer, vendor, or manufacturer, addressing the 'replaced commensurate with risk' requirement.
CA-7 develops a system-level continuous monitoring strategy and implements it with system-level metrics, directly operationalizing continuous monitoring that consumes the generated log records.
SI-4 monitors the system to detect attacks, indicators of potential attack, and unauthorized connections; identifies unauthorized use — supporting continuous monitoring informed by log records.
CM-10 (Software Usage Restrictions) tracks use of software, controls copying and distribution in line with licensing, partially preventing unauthorized installation and execution.

CM-11 (User-installed Software) directly governs installation of software by users through policies, enforcement mechanisms, and ongoing compliance monitoring, which fully prevents unauthorized software installation and execution.
CM-7 (Least Functionality) prohibits or restricts specified functions, ports, protocols, and software, partially preventing unauthorized software from running.
SI-16 (Memory Protection) protects system memory from unauthorized code execution, supporting the prevention goal.
SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity) detects unauthorized changes to software/firmware, supporting the prevention of unauthorized software installation.
CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring) establishes a continuous monitoring strategy with system-level metrics, supporting SDLC performance monitoring.
CM-3 (Configuration Change Control) reviews configuration-controlled changes with explicit consideration for security and privacy impacts, supporting secure SDLC integration.
PM-6 (Measures of Performance) develops, monitors, and reports on information security and privacy measures of performance, partially satisfying the monitoring portion.
AU-6 requires reporting audit findings to personnel or roles, providing a partial mechanism for communicating recovery status to designated stakeholders.

CP-2 develops a contingency plan that addresses contingency roles, responsibilities, and coordination, providing a vehicle for defining internal and external stakeholder communication during recovery.
The IR-8 plan describes the structure and organization of the incident response capability, supporting the designation of communication roles and processes for recovery progress updates.
CA-3 approves and manages information exchange between systems using agreements such as service-level or memoranda of agreement, which loosely underpins approved external/public messaging channels.
CP-2 develops a contingency plan that addresses contingency roles, responsibilities, and coordination with incident response, supporting the recovery portion of the incident response plan.

CP-2 develops a contingency plan that identifies essential mission and business functions, provides recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics. It directly supports the selection, scoping, prioritization, and performance of recovery actions.
RA-9 performs criticality analysis to identify critical system components and functions, enabling the organization to scope and prioritize recovery actions accordingly.
CP-10 provides for recovery and reconstitution of the system, using the verified restoration assets during the restoration process.

SI-7 employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software, firmware, and information, and specifies actions when unauthorized changes are detected. It directly supports verification of integrity of restoration assets before use.

CP-2 requires identification of essential mission and business functions and associated contingency requirements, supporting consideration of critical mission functions in post-incident operational norms.
RA-9 identifies critical system components and functions through criticality analysis, supporting identification of critical mission functions for post-incident operational norms.

AU-6 requires review and analysis of audit records for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity, providing evidentiary input that can support confirming normal operating status after recovery.

CP-4 tests the contingency plan and initiates corrective actions, supporting readiness to restore and confirm normal operating status. It enables but does not by itself perform post-restoration confirmation.

CP-9 mandates backups of user-level, system-level, and documentation information at defined frequencies, producing the source data required to restore systems and services. It enables but does not execute or verify restoration.

SI-7 requires employing integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software, firmware, and information. This capability can be applied to verify integrity of restored assets, but does not by itself cover restoration or normal-status confirmation.
IR-5 tracks and documents incidents, contributing to the completion of incident-related records but not addressing declaration-of-end criteria.

AU-6 requires reviewing and analyzing system audit records for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity and assessing potential impact, which underpins the analytical work to establish what occurred during an incident, though root-cause analysis as such is not explicit.

AU-11 retains audit records for a defined period to support after-the-fact investigations, which indirectly contributes to the integrity and provenance of investigation records by ensuring they remain available for review.

AU-3 ensures that audit records contain information establishing what type of event occurred, when, where, source, outcome, and identity of individuals/objects, which addresses recording actions performed during an investigation, though integrity preservation is not its primary focus.

AU-9 protects audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion and alerts on detection of such events, directly supporting preservation of integrity and provenance of investigation records.

IR-5 requires tracking and documenting incidents, directly addressing the recording of actions performed during an investigation, though integrity and provenance preservation are not explicitly covered by this control.
AU-12 provides audit record generation capability for defined event types on system components, which is the mechanism by which incident data and metadata are actually captured and collected.

AU-2 identifies the types of events that the system is capable of logging and coordinates the event logging function, which underpins the collection of incident data and metadata, though collection itself must be executed by AU-12/AU-3.

AU-3 specifies the content that audit records must contain (type, time, location, source, outcome, identity), defining the metadata fields that accompany incident data and thereby ensuring collected records carry meaningful metadata.

AU-9 protects audit information and audit logging tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion, directly preserving the integrity of collected incident data; provenance is supported by the alerting on detection of tampering.

IR-5 requires tracking and documenting incidents, contributing to the collection of incident data and metadata, though integrity and provenance preservation are not explicitly addressed by this control.
AU-11 Audit Record Retention preserves records to support after-the-fact investigations, enabling retrospective validation of incident magnitude.
AU-3 Content of Audit Records (type, time, location, source, outcome, identity) provides detailed evidence required to estimate and validate incident magnitude.
AU-7 Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation supports on-demand review and after-the-fact investigations, which enable magnitude estimation and validation.
IR-5 Incident Monitoring tracks and documents incidents, providing the records and ongoing visibility needed to estimate and validate incident magnitude.
AU-13 Monitoring for Information Disclosure requires notifying designated personnel or roles upon discovery of unauthorized information disclosure.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan describes the structure and organization of the response capability, which typically addresses communications and notification procedures.
PM-16 Threat Awareness Program implements a cross-organization information-sharing capability that supports awareness and notification across stakeholder groups.
SI-5 Security Alerts, Advisories, and Directives disseminates alerts to relevant personnel and external organizations, supporting incident notification.
AU-16 Cross-organizational Audit Logging coordinates audit information across organizational boundaries, enabling sharing of incident-related information externally.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan defines the structure and high-level approach for communication and information sharing during and after incidents.
PM-15 establishes contact with external security and privacy groups, supporting information exchange with external stakeholders.
PM-16 Threat Awareness Program explicitly implements a cross-organization information-sharing capability for threat intelligence.
SI-5 disseminates security alerts, advisories, and directives to designated personnel and external organizations, supporting information sharing.

IR-1 develops and disseminates incident response policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities, and management commitment, supporting formalized execution of the incident response plan.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability (preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery) consistent with the IR plan, partially covering execution once an incident is declared. However, the control coordinates with contingency planning rather than explicitly with relevant third parties.

AU-6 requires review and analysis of audit records for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity, which contributes evidence used during incident report triage and validation but does not perform the triage/validation itself.

IR-8's incident response plan describes a high-level approach for the incident response capability, which commonly defines how incidents are categorized and prioritized; coverage is supporting rather than direct.

IR-8's IR plan describes the structure and organization of the IR capability, typically including escalation roles and thresholds; coverage of the explicit 'as needed' escalation procedure is indirect.

CP-10 (System Recovery and Reconstitution) provides recovery to a known state consistent with recovery time and recovery point objectives after a disruption, compromise, or failure, directly enabling the recovery portion of the framework item, but it does not itself define or apply the criteria for initiating recovery from an incident.

CP-2 (Contingency Plan) provides recovery objectives, restoration priorities, and metrics, and addresses contingency roles and responsibilities, which form the basis for the criteria that trigger incident recovery, although the item concerns applying the criteria rather than just defining them.
AC-3 Access Enforcement enforces approved authorizations for logical access, helping contain an incident by preventing further unauthorized system access.
AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement controls the flow of information within and between systems based on flow control policies, limiting an incident's lateral expansion.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan provides a roadmap and high-level approach that typically details containment strategies.
PE-10 Emergency Shutoff provides the capability to shut off power to the system or specific components during emergencies, supporting physical containment of certain incident types.
SC-7 Boundary Protection monitors and controls communications at external and key internal managed interfaces, which helps contain incidents by isolating affected segments.
Retaining audit records supports after-the-fact investigations needed to scope eradication efforts and confirm that all traces of an incident have been removed from the system.
Plans of Action and Milestones document the planned remediation actions to correct weaknesses and reduce vulnerabilities discovered during incidents, supporting eradication of underlying causes.

System-level continuous monitoring supplies the ongoing visibility needed to detect any remnants of an incident and to verify that eradication has been successful and the system has returned to a known-good state.

Establishing and implementing secure configuration settings enables responders to restore affected components to a hardened baseline during eradication, removing attacker modifications and persistent threats.

The incident response policy establishes governance, scope, roles, and responsibilities for the incident response program, providing the policy foundation under which eradication activities are conducted.
Testing the effectiveness of the incident response capability helps validate that eradication procedures actually work as intended, supporting assurance that incidents are eradicated.
Tracking and documenting incidents enables responders to confirm when eradication is complete and to verify that eradicated threats do not reappear, supporting the eradication objective.

The incident response plan provides the roadmap, structure, and high-level approach for the incident response capability, including how eradication activities are organized and executed, thereby enabling the eradication of incidents.

hit.rationale: AU-6 requires reviewing and analyzing system audit records for indications of inappropriate or unusual activity, providing analysis of potentially adverse events but not fully characterizing all associated activities.
IR-4 incident handling explicitly includes detection and analysis as a phase for characterizing incidents, contributing to understanding the activities associated with adverse events.

SI-4 system monitoring detects and identifies unauthorized activity, producing the raw inputs that downstream analysis uses to understand associated activities, but does not itself perform the analysis.
AU-6 review and analysis of audit records draws upon multiple log sources across the system, supporting but not fully implementing correlation across sources.
SI-4 monitors the system across multiple vectors (local, network, remote) providing multi-source data feeds that can be correlated for adverse event detection.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability whose detection and analysis phases produce adverse event information that is then made available to responders. It enables rather than directly satisfies the dissemination requirement.

PM-16 establishes a threat awareness program that includes a cross-organization information-sharing capability for threat intelligence, providing the threat intelligence feed that is then integrated into analysis. It supplies the source intelligence but does not itself perform the integration into analysis workflows.

RA-10 establishes a cyber threat hunting capability that searches for indicators of compromise and detects, tracks, and disrupts threats that evade existing controls. This represents one form of contextual/threat-intelligence-informed analysis but does not by itself define the broader integration of all contextual information.

RA-3 risk assessments identify threats and vulnerabilities, supplying contextual information (threat sources, likelihood) that can be integrated into adverse event analysis. It supports but does not satisfy the integration requirement on its own.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability that includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery — providing the operational mechanism by which adverse events are evaluated against criteria and declared as incidents. It performs the declaration activity but relies on the plan for the criteria themselves.

IR-8 develops an incident response plan that provides the roadmap and high-level approach for the incident response capability, including how incidents are declared and the criteria involved. The plan defines the framework for declaration; execution requires IR-4 and related controls.
AU-12 Audit Record Generation provides the underlying audit record generation capability that enables network monitoring for adverse events.
CA-7 Continuous Monitoring establishes a system-level continuous monitoring strategy with metrics that enables ongoing detection of adverse events on networks.
SC-5 DoS Protection employs controls to achieve denial-of-service objectives, which is one type of adverse event monitored on networks.

SC-7 Boundary Protection monitors and controls communications at external and key internal managed interfaces, directly supporting network monitoring for adverse events but not addressing all network services comprehensively.

SI-4 System Monitoring explicitly requires monitoring the system to detect attacks, indicators of potential attacks, and unauthorized local, network, and remote connections, which fully satisfies monitoring of networks and network services for adverse events.
PE-20 Asset Monitoring and Tracking employs asset location technologies to track and monitor movement of assets within controlled areas, supporting physical environment monitoring.
PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access monitors physical access to the facility to detect and respond to physical security incidents, covering physical environment monitoring for adverse events.
AU-12 Audit Record Generation provides the audit record generation capability that underpins monitoring of personnel activity and technology usage.
CA-7 Continuous Monitoring implements a system-level continuous monitoring strategy with metrics, providing the framework for monitoring external service providers.

PS-7 External Personnel Security establishes security roles and responsibilities for external providers and requires compliance with personnel security policies, supporting oversight of external service provider activities.

SA-9 External System Services requires providers of external system services to comply with organizational security requirements and defines oversight roles, enabling monitoring of external service provider activities.
AU-12 provides audit record generation capability across system components, supplying the underlying telemetry data required for monitoring hardware, software, runtime environments, and their data.
CA-7 establishes a system-level continuous monitoring strategy and metrics, providing the operational framework that enables ongoing monitoring of systems for adverse events.

SI-4 directly requires monitoring the system to detect attacks and indicators of potential attacks, unauthorized local/network/remote connections, and unauthorized use of the system, fully satisfying the monitoring of computing hardware/software, runtime environments, and data to find adverse events.

PM-11 requires defining organizational mission and business processes with consideration for information security and privacy and the resulting risk, directly tying mission understanding to cybersecurity risk management. It does not by itself describe how the mission informs risk decisions end-to-end, so partial coverage.

PM-8 addresses information security and privacy issues in the development, documentation, and updating of a critical infrastructure and key resources protection plan, addressing criticality identification and documentation. Communication to external stakeholders and their expectations are not explicitly covered.

RA-9 requires identifying critical system components and functions via criticality analysis at SDLC decision points, directly supporting identification of critical capabilities and services. It does not address communication to external stakeholders or their expectations.

PM-11 requires defining organizational mission and business processes with consideration for information security and privacy, and determining information protection needs associated with them. This directly contributes to understanding the outcomes, capabilities, and services the organization depends on, though it does not by itself mandate external communication of those dependencies.

SA-9 requires the organization to oversee external system service providers and define roles and responsibilities with regard to them. This directly supports understanding which external services the organization depends on and documenting those dependencies.

PM-9 Risk Management Strategy establishes the comprehensive cybersecurity risk management strategy whose outcomes are reviewed; however it focuses on strategy creation rather than the periodic outcome review that informs adjustment.
PM-30 Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy develops an organization-wide strategy for managing supply chain risks, contributing to the broader risk-coverage domain that GV.OV-02 reviews.

PM-9 Risk Management Strategy develops and manages the comprehensive cybersecurity risk management strategy that is the subject of periodic review and adjustment, though it does not, on its own, mandate the review cadence.

PM-4 Plan of Action and Milestones Process implements a process to develop and maintain POAMs documenting remedial actions to address identified deficiencies, providing the concrete adjustment workflow referenced in GV.OV-03.

PM-6 Measures of Performance requires developing, monitoring, and reporting on the results of information security and privacy measures of performance, providing the principal mechanism for evaluating cybersecurity risk management performance.

PM-1 Information Security Program Plan requires development and dissemination of an organization-wide security program plan that provides overview and describes controls, supporting the 'communicated' aspect of the policy lifecycle.

RA-1 Policy and Procedures codifies the develop, document, disseminate, review, and update cycle for risk assessment policy. It supports the lifecycle mechanics called out in GV.PO-02, though scoped to risk assessment rather than all cybersecurity risk policy.

PM-9 requires developing a comprehensive strategy to manage security and privacy risk associated with organizational systems. This strategy typically defines risk management objectives, though the control does not explicitly require documented stakeholder agreement.

PM-9 (Risk Management Strategy) requires a comprehensive strategy to manage security and privacy risk. Such a strategy typically establishes, communicates, and maintains risk appetite and tolerance, though the control does not prescribe the formal statement format.

PM-9 requires a comprehensive strategy to manage security risk to organizational operations, assets, individuals, other organizations, and the Nation. By establishing an organization-wide risk management strategy, this integrates cybersecurity risk management into the broader enterprise risk context.

PM-28 (Risk Framing) documents the assumptions, constraints, priorities, and trade-offs that shape which 'risk response options' the organization considers appropriate. It supports strategic risk response decision-making but does not deliver the communications aspect of the item.

PM-9 develops a comprehensive strategy to manage security and privacy risk at the organizational level. It establishes the strategic direction against which risk responses are framed, but it does not by itself enumerate specific 'appropriate risk response options' or address how those options are 'communicated'.

PM-30 (Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy) develops an organization-wide strategy for managing supply chain risks associated with the development, acquisition, maintenance, and disposal of systems, components, and services, directly addressing the third-party portion of the communication requirement.

PM-28 (Risk Framing) explicitly documents the priorities and trade-offs the organization considers when managing risk, supporting the 'prioritizing' element of a standardized risk calculation method. It does not by itself establish the calculating or categorizing methods.

PM-9 (Risk Management Strategy) develops a comprehensive strategy integrating security and privacy risk management at the organization level, providing the umbrella under which standardized risk calculation, documentation, categorization, and prioritization methods are institutionalized and disseminated.

RA-3 (Risk Assessment) identifies threats and vulnerabilities and determines the likelihood and magnitude of harm, providing the quantitative 'calculating' basis that a standardized risk method requires. It also documents assessment results, contributing to the 'documenting' element.

PM-28 (Risk Framing) considers priorities and trade-offs when managing risk, which provides a structural hook for including positive risks; however, it does not explicitly characterize strategic opportunities, so it is only enabling rather than satisfying.

PM-9 (Risk Management Strategy) provides the comprehensive organizational framework in which all categories of risk, including positive opportunities, would be discussed. It enables inclusion of opportunities but does not characterize them.

RA-3 (Risk Assessment) conducts assessment of risk, generating inputs that feed risk discussions; it does not itself characterize positive risks, only enabling the discussion by providing assessment outputs.

PM-2 appoints a senior agency information security officer with the mission and resources to coordinate, develop, implement, and maintain an organization-wide information security program, establishing leadership responsibility for cybersecurity.

PM-29 (Risk Management Program Leadership Roles) appoints a Senior Accountable Official for Risk Management to align information security and privacy management with strategic, operational, and budgetary planning processes, and establishes a Risk Executive function — directly assigning leadership accountability for cybersecurity risk.
PM-23 establishes a Data Governance Body consisting of defined roles with responsibilities, which helps institutionalize responsibility and authority structures.
PM-29 establishes a Risk Executive function and appoints a Senior Accountable Official for Risk Management, defining specific roles and authorities for cybersecurity risk management.

PM-3 (Information Security and Privacy Resources) explicitly requires including the resources needed to implement the information security and privacy programs in capital planning and investment requests, fully addressing resource allocation.
PM-13 establishes a security and privacy workforce development and improvement program, directly integrating cybersecurity into workforce/HR practices.

PS-1 (Personnel Security Policy and Procedures) develops and disseminates personnel security policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, responsibilities — embedding cybersecurity into HR-related personnel security practices.

PS-7 (External Personnel Security) establishes personnel security requirements for external providers and requires compliance with personnel security policies — extending cybersecurity into HR practices for contractors.

PM-30 (Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy) develops an organization-wide strategy for managing supply chain risks with consistent implementation, satisfying the strategy portion and partially the objectives/policies/processes.
SR-2 (Supply Chain Risk Management Plan) develops a plan for managing supply chain risks across the full life cycle, supplying the program/plan layer of the framework item.
SR-3 establishes a process or processes to identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements, satisfying the processes component of the framework item.
PM-30 requires implementation of the SCRM strategy consistently across the organization, demonstrating integration with the wider cybersecurity program.
PM-31 establishes an organization-wide continuous monitoring strategy, providing the ongoing improvement process that feeds assessment of SCRM integration.
PM-9 develops a comprehensive risk management strategy covering security risk to operations and assets, the umbrella into which SCRM risk management is integrated.
RA-7 (Risk Response) responds to findings from assessments, monitoring and audits, closing the improvement loop for SCRM integration.

RA-9 (Criticality Analysis) identifies critical system components and functions via criticality analysis at SDLC decision points, supplying the prioritization methodology referenced in the framework item.

SR-6 assesses and reviews supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers/contractors at a defined frequency, directly producing both supplier awareness and risk-based prioritization by criticality.
SA-4 (Acquisition Process) requires security and privacy requirements to be included in acquisition contracts using standardized contract language, directly addressing contract integration.
SR-5 mandates the use of acquisition strategies, contract tools, and procurement methods to protect against, identify, and mitigate supply chain risks, supporting contractual integration.

SR-6 requires assessing and reviewing supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers, contractors, and their provided systems/components, performing the due diligence before/during the relationship.
SR-3 establishes processes to identify and address weaknesses or deficiencies in supply chain elements and employs controls to protect against supply chain threats, addressing risk response.
SR-6 directly assesses and reviews supply chain-related risks from suppliers/contractors over time, fulfilling the understand, record, prioritize, assess, and monitor functions for third-party risks.
SA-9 requires external service providers to comply with organizational security/privacy requirements and defines oversight and user roles, supporting third-party integration into incident response.
SR-8 establishes agreements with supply chain entities for notification of compromises and assessment results, enabling third-party participation in incident coordination.

PM-30 requires developing an organization-wide supply chain risk management strategy aligned with and implemented consistently across the organization's processes. It directly addresses integrating supply chain security practices but does not by itself cover lifecycle performance monitoring.
PM-31 establishes the organization-wide continuous monitoring strategy with metrics and frequencies, providing the governance frame for performance monitoring that includes supply chain practices.

PM-9 requires a comprehensive strategy to manage security and privacy risk across organizational operations, supporting the enterprise risk management integration component. It is not supply-chain specific.

SR-2 explicitly covers risks associated with research and development, design, manufacturing, acquisition, delivery, integration, operations and maintenance, and disposal—spanning the full technology lifecycle. It does not by itself address ERM integration or ongoing performance monitoring.

SR-3 establishes processes to identify and address weaknesses or deficiencies in supply chain elements, supporting integration of supply chain security practices. It enables monitoring but does not on its own describe monitoring frequency or ERM alignment.

SR-6 requires assessing and reviewing supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers on a defined frequency, directly supporting ongoing performance monitoring of supply chain security practices.

SR-2 covers risks across disposal—the lifecycle phase occurring after conclusion of a service agreement—and is the supply chain risk management plan itself. It addresses post-partnership activities at a high level, but does not explicitly enumerate post-termination provisions.

SR-3 establishes processes to address weaknesses in supply chain elements; such processes can be designed to continue after a supplier relationship ends, supporting post-partnership supply chain risk handling.

SR-5 requires employing acquisition strategies, contract tools, and procurement methods to mitigate supply chain risk. Contract tools can specifically include end-of-life and post-termination provisions, enabling the framework item.

CM-8 requires developing and documenting an inventory of system components that accurately reflects the system; hardware components are explicitly within its scope, making it a direct, full match for maintaining hardware inventories.

PM-5 requires developing and updating an inventory of organizational systems, which by extension includes hardware, but does not enumerate hardware specifically or include component-level detail expected by ID.AM-01.

CM-8's inventory of system components explicitly includes software (e.g., operating systems, applications, firmware) and the systems themselves, fully covering software, services, and systems inventory requirements.
PM-5 maintains an inventory of organizational systems, partially satisfying the systems portion of this item, but does not explicitly cover software or services inventories at the component level.

AC-4 enforces approved authorizations for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems based on information flow control policies, partially satisfying the data flow representation requirement.

CA-3 approves and manages the exchange of information between the system and other systems using interconnection security agreements or similar arrangements, supporting the documentation of inter-system data flows.
CA-9 requires authorizing internal connections and documenting the interface characteristics and nature of information communicated, supporting representation of internal data flows.

SA-9 requires external system service providers to comply with organizational requirements and defines oversight and user roles, addressing services provided by suppliers but not a formal inventory on its own.
RA-9 (Criticality Analysis) directly identifies critical system components and functions through criticality analysis, covering the 'criticality' and prioritization aspects of asset prioritization.

CM-12 (Information Location) identifies and documents the location of information and the specific system components on which information is processed/stored, plus users with access, contributing to data inventory and metadata.
CM-13 (Data Action Mapping) develops and documents a map of system data actions, providing an inventory-like representation of data and metadata relationships within the system.
CM-9 (Configuration Management Plan) establishes a process for identifying configuration items throughout the SDLC, supporting life cycle oversight of hardware/software.
SA-3 (System Development Life Cycle) acquires, develops, and manages the system using a SDLC that incorporates security and privacy considerations, directly addressing lifecycle management.
SI-18 (PII Quality Operations) explicitly checks accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness of personally identifiable information across the information life cycle.
SR-12 (Component Disposal) addresses the disposal phase by requiring defined techniques and methods for disposing data, documentation, tools, or system components at end-of-life.

CA-2 requires developing control assessment plans and conducting assessments of controls using appropriate assessors. This is the primary evaluation mechanism that produces findings from which improvements are identified. Partial because CA-2 generates findings but does not itself mandate the identification of improvements (handled via CA-5).

CA-5 requires developing a Plan of Action and Milestones to document planned remediation actions to correct weaknesses identified during assessments. This is the principal mechanism for tracking improvements from evaluations. Partial because it requires inputs from other evaluations such as CA-2.

RA-3 requires conducting a risk assessment that identifies threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, and magnitude. It supports the framework item as one form of evaluation whose findings feed into improvement identification.

RA-7 requires responding to findings from security and privacy assessments, monitoring, and audits in accordance with organizational risk tolerance. This drives improvement identification from evaluations. Partial because it acts on findings generated by other evaluations.

CA-8 requires conducting penetration testing on systems or components. Penetration testing is a security test whose findings lead to improvement identification. Partial because it covers penetration testing specifically rather than the full range of security tests and exercises.

CP-4 requires testing the contingency plan using defined tests and initiating corrective actions from results. This is a security exercise producing improvement findings. Partial because it covers contingency plan testing only.
IR-3 requires testing the effectiveness of the incident response capability. This is a security exercise whose findings lead to improvements. Partial because it covers incident response testing only.

RA-5 requires monitoring and scanning for vulnerabilities in systems and hosted applications, including when new vulnerabilities are identified. This is a security test producing improvement findings. Partial because it covers vulnerability monitoring and scanning specifically.

SA-11 requires the developer to perform unit, integration, regression, and/or system testing during post-design stages. This is a security test producing improvement findings. Partial because it covers developer-side testing only.

CA-7 implements a system-level continuous monitoring strategy that includes ongoing metrics monitoring and assessment of controls. This is an operational activity whose findings lead to improvement identification. Partial because it covers continuous monitoring specifically.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability covering preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery. This operational process produces findings that lead to improvement identification. Partial because it covers incident handling specifically.

PM-31 implements organization-wide continuous monitoring programs with defined metrics and frequencies. This is an operational activity producing improvement findings. Partial because it covers the strategy-level continuous monitoring activity.

CP-2 requires developing a contingency plan identifying essential mission and business functions, recovery objectives, roles, and responsibilities, qualifying it as one of the 'other cybersecurity plans that affect operations' that must be established.

IR-8 requires developing an incident response plan that provides a roadmap, structure, and high-level approach, which directly establishes the incident response plan. However, it does not by itself cover the communication, maintenance, and improvement aspects of the framework item.

PL-2 requires development of security and privacy plans for the system that describe operational context, components, and connections, making it one of the 'other cybersecurity plans that affect operations' that must be established.
RA-3 (Risk Assessment) includes identifying threats to and vulnerabilities in the system, contributing to vulnerability identification within a broader risk assessment process.
RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning) directly monitors and scans for vulnerabilities in the system and hosted applications, identifying and recording vulnerabilities on an ongoing basis.

PM-15 establishes and institutionalizes contact with selected groups and associations within the security and privacy communities, which directly supports receiving threat intelligence from information sharing forums and sources. However, it does not itself cover receiving cyber threat intelligence broadly, so it is only partial.

PM-16 implements a threat awareness program that includes a cross-organization information-sharing capability for threat intelligence, directly addressing receipt of threat intelligence from sharing forums. Partial because it does not by itself cover the full set of external sources.

SI-5 requires receiving system security alerts, advisories, and directives from external organizations on an ongoing basis, directly supporting intake of threat intelligence. Partial because it focuses on alerts/advisories/directives rather than the full scope of forums and sources.

PM-16's threat awareness program supports identification of threats organization-wide by institutionalizing cross-organization information sharing, but it does not directly identify/record internal and external threats to the organization, so it is supporting only.

RA-3 explicitly requires conducting a risk assessment that includes identifying threats to the system, including internal and external threats. It also implies recording through assessment documentation, so it fully satisfies the item.

RA-3 requires determining the likelihood and magnitude of harm from threat exploitation of vulnerabilities, which directly maps to potential impacts and likelihoods of threats exploiting vulnerabilities. Combined with identifying threats and vulnerabilities, it fully satisfies the item.

RA-3 conducts a risk assessment that integrates threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts to determine risk, partially addressing understanding inherent risk and prioritization. It is partial because RA-3 focuses on assessment rather than explicit prioritization of response actions.

RA-7 requires responding to findings from security and privacy assessments, monitoring, and audits in accordance with organizational risk tolerance, directly informing risk response prioritization. Partial because it does not itself combine threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods, and impacts.
PM-9 (Risk Management Strategy) develops a comprehensive strategy to manage security and privacy risk, which supports the planning and communication of risk responses organization-wide.

RA-7 (Risk Response) directly addresses responding to findings from assessments, monitoring, and audits in accordance with organizational risk tolerance, which constitutes the core act of choosing and executing risk responses. However, it does not by itself cover prioritization, planning, tracking, and communication of those responses.

CM-3 (Configuration Change Control) determines types of changes, reviews proposed changes, and approves/disapproves them with explicit consideration for security and privacy impacts. It directly covers the 'managed' and 'assessed for risk impact' portions of the framework item for configuration-controlled changes.

CM-4 (Impact Analyses) requires analyzing changes to the system to determine potential security and privacy impacts prior to change implementation, directly supporting the assessment of changes for risk impact.

RA-5 (Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning) monitors and scans for vulnerabilities in the system and hosted applications and when new vulnerabilities are identified, which directly supports the analysis and response aspects of vulnerability disclosure handling.

SA-4 (Acquisition Process) includes security and privacy requirements, descriptions, and criteria in acquisition contracts using standardized language, supporting pre-acquisition assessment of authenticity and integrity requirements.

SI-7 (Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity) employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to software, firmware, and information, directly supporting integrity assessment of hardware and software.

SR-11 (Component Authenticity) develops and implements anti-counterfeit policy and procedures that include means to detect and prevent counterfeit components from entering the system, directly addressing authenticity assessment of hardware.

SR-6 (Supplier Assessments and Reviews) assesses and reviews supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers and the components/services they provide, supporting pre-acquisition authenticity and integrity assessment of hardware and software.

SR-6 explicitly requires assessing and reviewing supply chain-related risks associated with suppliers or contractors, directly covering the 'suppliers are assessed' portion of the framework item. Partial because SR-6 does not specifically limit scope to 'critical' suppliers nor require the assessment 'prior to acquisition'.

AC-2 (Account Management) covers identity/account provisioning, role membership, and lifecycle, partially satisfying the identities-managed aspect of PR.AA-01 but does not by itself cover hardware/service credentials or authenticator binding.

IA-4 (Identifier Management) directly governs how individual, group, role, service, and device identifiers are authorized, selected, assigned, and managed, fully satisfying the identity-lifecycle management aspect of PR.AA-01.

IA-5 (Authenticator Management) governs the full lifecycle of credentials (verification, distribution, content, recovery) for users, services, and devices, fully satisfying the credential-management aspect of PR.AA-01.

IA-12 (Identity Proofing) directly addresses proofing users to appropriate identity assurance levels, resolving identities to unique individuals, and collecting/validating attributes—the core of PR.AA-02.
IA-10 (Adaptive Authentication) requires supplemental authentication under specific circumstances, strengthening PR.AA-03 authentication assurance but not satisfying it alone.
IA-11 (Re-authentication) supports PR.AA-03 by requiring users to re-authenticate in defined circumstances, reinforcing ongoing authentication assurance.
IA-2 uniquely identifies and authenticates organizational users and binds that identification to processes acting on their behalf, fully satisfying the user-authentication portion of PR.AA-03.

IA-3 (Device Identification and Authentication) uniquely identifies and authenticates devices before establishing local, remote, or network connections, fully satisfying the hardware-authentication portion of PR.AA-03.
IA-8 uniquely identifies and authenticates non-organizational users and processes, partially extending PR.AA-03's authentication coverage to external user populations.

IA-9 (Service Identification and Authentication) uniquely identifies and authenticates services and applications before establishing communications, fully satisfying the service-authentication portion of PR.AA-03.

IA-13 (Identity Providers and Authorization Servers) supplies the infrastructure that issues, conveys, and verifies identity assertions, enabling PR.AA-04 but not by itself providing the cryptographic protection or transport.

AC-1 requires developing, documenting, and disseminating an access control policy that addresses purpose, scope, roles, and responsibilities. This directly satisfies the requirement that access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations be defined in a policy, but does not address the management, enforcement, review, or the principles of least privilege and separation of duties.

AC-2 Account Management defines and documents the types of accounts allowed/prohibited, assigns account managers, requires prerequisites for group/role membership, and specifies authorized users and group/role membership. This directly addresses the management and periodic review of access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations.

AC-24 Access Control Decisions establishes procedures and implements mechanisms to ensure access control decisions are applied to each access request prior to access enforcement. It does not by itself satisfy the item but enables consistent enforcement of access decisions.

AC-3 Access Enforcement enforces approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies. This directly satisfies the enforcement aspect of access permissions, entitlements, and authorizations.

AC-5 Separation of Duties identifies and documents duties of individuals and defines system access authorizations to support separation of duties. This directly satisfies the separation of duties principle requirement in PR.AA-05.

AC-6 Least Privilege employs the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized accesses for users (or processes acting on behalf of users) that are necessary to accomplish assigned organizational tasks. This directly satisfies the least privilege principle requirement in PR.AA-05.

PE-2 Physical Access Authorizations develops, approves, and maintains a list of individuals with authorized access to the facility, issues authorization credentials, and reviews the access list at a defined frequency. This directly addresses the management aspect of physical access.

PE-3 Physical Access Control enforces physical access authorizations at entry and exit points by verifying individual access authorizations before granting access and controlling ingress/egress using physical systems, devices, or guards. This directly satisfies the enforcement aspect of physical access.

PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access monitors physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents; reviews physical access logs and coordinates results with the organizational incident response capability. This addresses the monitoring aspect of physical access.

AT-2 Literacy Training and Awareness provides security and privacy literacy training to system users (including managers, senior executives, and contractors) as part of initial training and at a defined frequency thereafter. This directly satisfies the requirement that personnel be provided with awareness and training to perform general tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind.

AT-3 Role-based Training provides role-based security and privacy training to personnel with defined roles and responsibilities before authorizing access and at a defined frequency. This directly satisfies the requirement that individuals in specialized roles receive awareness and training to possess the knowledge and skills for relevant tasks with cybersecurity risks in mind.
MP-8 Media Downgrading ensures media holding data is properly sanitized or destroyed before disposal or reuse, supporting confidentiality of data-at-rest at end-of-life.

SC-13 Cryptographic Protection provides the cryptographic mechanisms (e.g., encryption) that enable confidentiality and integrity protection for data-at-rest, but does not itself implement the storage-layer protection.
SC-28 Protection of Information at Rest is the primary control designed to protect the confidentiality and integrity of data at rest, directly fulfilling the framework item's requirement.
SI-7 Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity uses integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to stored information, supporting the integrity aspect of data-at-rest protection.
SC-13 Cryptographic Protection provides the cryptographic mechanisms (e.g., TLS) needed to implement SC-8 and protect transmitted data, but does not itself enforce the transport-layer protection.
SC-40 Wireless Link Protection extends in-transit protection to wireless links against signal-parameter attacks, supporting the broader in-transit confidentiality/integrity objective.
SC-8 Transmission Confidentiality and Integrity is the primary control that protects the confidentiality and integrity of data-in-transit, directly fulfilling this framework item.

SC-39 Process Isolation maintains separate execution domains for processes, which directly addresses confidentiality and integrity of data-in-use by preventing cross-process interference, but does not address availability.

SI-16 Memory Protection implements controls to protect system memory from unauthorized code execution, directly supporting integrity of data-in-use, but only partially addresses the full CIA requirement.
CP-6 Alternate Storage Site ensures backup information is stored with controls equivalent to the primary site and can be retrieved, supporting the 'protected' and 'maintained' aspects of backup data.

CP-9 System Backup is the primary control that establishes the creation, protection, and maintenance of backups of user-level, system-level, and documentation information, directly fulfilling this framework item.
AC-3 (Access Enforcement) enforces approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources, partially protecting networks/environments from unauthorized logical access.
PE-14 (Environmental Controls) maintains temperature, humidity, pressure, and radiation levels and monitors them at defined frequencies, partially protecting assets from environmental threats.
PE-15 (Water Damage Protection) protects the system from damage resulting from water leakage via master shutoff or isolation valves, partially addressing a specific environmental threat.
PE-18 (Location of System Components) positions system components to minimize potential damage from physical and environmental hazards, partially protecting assets.
PE-23 (Facility Location) plans the facility site considering physical and environmental hazards, partially protecting assets from environmental threats.
PE-9 (Power Equipment and Cabling) protects power equipment and cabling from damage and destruction, supporting protection from environmental threats.
SC-6 protects resource availability through priority, quota, and control allocation, providing a mechanism underpinning resilience in both normal and adverse conditions.
PM-3 requires including resources needed for information security and privacy programs in capital planning, enabling adequate organizational resource capacity.

CM-1 requires the organization to develop, document, and disseminate a configuration management policy addressing purpose, scope, roles, and responsibilities, which directly establishes the foundation for configuration management practices.

CM-2 requires developing, documenting, maintaining under configuration control, and reviewing a current baseline configuration, which is a core practice that both establishes the configuration and applies it operationally.
CM-3 mandates configuration change control with documented reviews and explicit consideration of security/privacy impacts, applying configuration management discipline to proposed changes.
CM-6 establishes and documents mandatory configuration settings, implements them, and tracks/verifies them — directly applying configuration management practices to system components.

CM-7 configures the system to provide only mission-essential capabilities and prohibits/restricts specific functions, ports, protocols, software and services, applying configuration principles to enforce least functionality.

CM-9 requires a configuration management plan that addresses roles, responsibilities, processes and procedures; this both establishes and operationalizes (applies) configuration management for the system.
CM-11 establishes policies governing user installation of software, enforces them, and monitors compliance, which enables removal or replacement of unauthorized software.

SI-2 requires identifying, reporting, and correcting system flaws and installing security-relevant software/firmware updates within an organization-defined time period, which is a core software maintenance practice commensurate with risk.
AU-11 retains audit records for a defined time period to support after-the-fact investigations and meet retention requirements, keeping log records available over time for continuous monitoring use.
AU-12 provides the audit record generation capability for auditable event types on system components and allows personnel to select which event types are logged, directly generating log records.
AU-3 ensures that generated audit records contain sufficient information (what, when, where, source, outcome, identity) to support their use, enabling the records generated to be fit for purpose.
AU-6 requires reviewing and analyzing audit records and reporting findings to designated personnel, making records available for review as part of monitoring.
SC-34 (Non-modifiable Executable Programs) loads applications from hardware-enforced, read-only media, partially preventing unauthorized software execution.
SA-11 (Developer Testing and Evaluation) requires ongoing security/privacy control assessments at post-design SDLC stages, partially addressing secure development and monitoring throughout the SDLC.

SA-3 (System Development Life Cycle) acquires, develops, and manages the system using an SDLC that incorporates security and privacy considerations, directly integrating secure development practices across the SDLC.
IR-4 coordinates incident handling activities with contingency planning, supporting the communication of recovery activities and progress to relevant parties during the response lifecycle.
CP-2's contingency plan can include coordination with external parties and approved messaging roles, providing weak support for sharing approved public updates during recovery.

CP-10 provides for the recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state consistent with recovery time and recovery point objectives, supporting the operational recovery activities called for by the incident response plan.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability consistent with the incident response plan that explicitly includes 'recovery' alongside preparation, detection and analysis, containment, and eradication. It covers the execution of the recovery actions once initiated from the incident response process.

IR-8 requires development of an incident response plan that provides a roadmap for implementing the incident response capability, including recovery activities. It establishes the plan whose recovery portion is executed.
IR-4 implements incident handling that includes recovery, supporting the performance of recovery actions within the overall incident lifecycle.
CP-9 conducts backups of user-level information, system-level information, and system documentation at defined frequencies, producing the restoration assets whose integrity must be verified.

PM-11 requires the organization to define mission and business processes with consideration for information security and privacy and the resulting risk, supporting consideration of critical mission functions when establishing post-incident operational norms.
PM-9 develops a comprehensive strategy to manage security risk to organizational operations and assets, supporting the consideration of cybersecurity risk management in post-incident norms.

CP-10 requires providing for the recovery and reconstitution of the system to a known state, directly supporting the restoration of systems and services. It does not explicitly cover integrity verification of restored assets or confirmation of normal operating status.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability spanning preparation through recovery, which entails recording incident activity documentation as recovery concludes. It addresses recovery-stage documentation but not the formal declaration criteria.

IR-8 develops an incident response plan that describes the high-level approach and structure of the response capability, which can embed the criteria used to declare the end of recovery. It does not by itself complete incident-related documentation.

AU-7 provides an audit record reduction and report generation capability that supports on-demand review and after-the-fact investigations, enabling the analysis referenced in the framework item without directly performing the root-cause analysis itself.

IR-4 mandates detection and analysis as part of the incident handling lifecycle, directly addressing 'Analysis is performed to establish what has taken place during an incident'; root-cause determination is supported but the control does not by itself prescribe formal root-cause analysis methodology.

IR-4 Incident Handling explicitly includes 'detection and analysis' activities, which directly support estimating the magnitude of an incident. However, it does not explicitly mandate validation of the magnitude estimate, so it is partial.
IR-8 Incident Response Plan provides a roadmap including the high-level approach for incident analysis, supporting magnitude estimation and validation processes.
RA-3 Risk Assessment determines 'magnitude of harm' from threats, which informs the framework for assessing incident magnitude during analysis.

IR-6 Incident Reporting requires internal personnel to report suspected incidents to the response capability within a defined time period, and requires reporting incident information to external authorities. This covers both internal and external notification but does not address all stakeholders.
IR-6 Incident Reporting requires sharing of incident information both internally (with the response capability) and externally (with authorities), directly enabling stakeholder information sharing.

IR-8 develops an incident response plan describing structure, organization, and high-level approach for the IR capability, providing the basis for execution, though execution in coordination with third parties is not directly addressed in the control text.

IR-4 includes 'detection and analysis' within incident handling, which is the operational analog of triaging and validating incident reports. Coverage is partial because explicit triage and validation steps are not enumerated in the control text.
IR-5 tracks and documents incidents, providing the records pipeline that supports triage and validation activities but does not itself perform those triage/validation functions.

IR-6 requires personnel to report suspected incidents to the organizational incident response capability within a defined time period, which supplies the incident reports that downstream triage and validation will process.

IR-4's detection and analysis phase of incident handling is the conventional locus for categorization and prioritization. The control text references these activities implicitly but does not explicitly require categorization/prioritization steps.
IR-5 tracks and documents incidents, providing the traceability and metadata needed to perform categorization and prioritization but not performing those classifications directly.

IR-4 implements incident handling including containment, eradication, and recovery, which implies escalation pathways, but the control text does not explicitly require a defined escalation or elevation process as needed.
IR-7 provides an incident response support resource offering advice and assistance to users, which can inform decisions to escalate or elevate incidents but does not itself operationalize escalation.

IR-4 implements an incident handling capability that explicitly includes recovery as a phase (alongside preparation, detection and analysis, containment, and eradication), so it supports applying criteria for initiating incident recovery, though the specific criteria themselves would need to be defined in the IR plan or CP-2.

IR-4 Incident Handling explicitly includes 'containment' as a defined phase, alongside eradication and recovery. While containment is named, dedicated containment controls/methods are not specified in the control text.

IR-4 explicitly requires that the incident handling capability includes 'preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, and recovery,' directly mandating that incidents are eradicated as a formal step of the response process.
